title: Continuous division by a uniformizer power
statement: Let $\ell$ be prime and let $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ be finite with valuation ring $A=\mathcal O_E$, valuation topology, and uniformizer $\pi$ [def-weil-l-adic-coefficient-extension]. For every $e\geq0$, multiplication by $\pi^e$ is a homeomorphism from $A$ onto the subspace $\pi^eA\subseteq E$. Consequently, if $T$ is a topological space and $f:T\to A$ is continuous with $f(t)\in\pi^eA$ for all $t$, there is a unique continuous $q:T\to A$ with $\pi^e q(t)=f(t)$. If $f(t_0)\in\pi^eA^\times$, then $q(t_0)\in A^\times$, and after restricting to an open neighbourhood of $t_0$, $q$ takes values in $A^\times$ and $q^{-1}$ is entrywise continuous.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 6.12(2), finite E case, pp. 18–19: continuous integral division and elementary pivot elimination; the displayed auxiliary statement is written out here because HRS uses it as a standard calculation.

proof.text: The valuation topology makes $E$ a topological field. Since a uniformizer is nonzero, multiplication by $\pi^e$ on $E$ is a homeomorphism with inverse multiplication by $\pi^{-e}$. Restricting this map to $A$ gives a homeomorphism $A\to\pi^eA$ with the subspace topology. Define $q$ as the inverse of this restriction composed with $f$; it is continuous and $A$-valued by the divisibility hypothesis, and it is unique because multiplication by $\pi^e$ is injective.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 6.12(2), finite E case, pp. 18–19: comparison of valuations makes division integral.

proof.text: Write $f(t_0)=\pi^e u$ with $u\in A^\times$. The defining equation $\pi^e q(t_0)=f(t_0)$ and cancellation of the nonzero element $\pi^e$ in the field $E$ give $q(t_0)=u$, so $q(t_0)$ is a unit of $A$.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 6.12(2), finite E case, pp. 18–19: comparison of valuations makes division integral.

proof.text: The unit group $A^\times$ is open in the valuation topology: for a unit $u$, the coset $u+\mathfrak m_E$ consists of units and is an open neighbourhood of $u$. Hence $U=q^{-1}(A^\times)$ is an open neighbourhood of $t_0$ and $q|_U$ is unit-valued. Inversion on $E^\times$ is continuous for the valuation topology, so $t\mapsto q(t)^{-1}$, viewed as an $A$-valued map on $U$, is continuous. This proves the final local assertion.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 6.12(2), finite E case, pp. 18–19: comparison of valuations makes division integral.

I read the item in full: its statement and its 3 steps. The only node it cites is def-weil-l-adic-coefficient-extension: clause 1 (the absolute value), clause 2 (O_E and m_E = {|x|<1}) and clause 3 (uniformizer with pi O_E = m_E, so pi is nonzero). I also read the consumer lem-sfb-continuous-integral-pivot-splitting: its step 1 needs exactly the entrywise quotient, the unit at t0 and the local continuous inverse, and this statement gives all three. I read the unit sk-def-sfb-dc-restricted-functors, the chapter sec-six-functors-basics, and the via chain up to lem-sfb-dc-hom-preserves. Source: HRS arXiv 2305.18131, proof of Thm 6.12(2), pp. 18-19 ('Comparing valuations ... a,b in Gamma(S,O_E)'). That is the same division argument, and proof_origin=agent is correct because HRS does not state the unit or inverse clause. The statement is true. Multiplication by pi^e is a homeomorphism of E (inverse: multiplication by pi^{-e}) and restricts to a homeomorphism A -> pi^e A, so q is continuous and unique. If f(t0) = pi^e u then q(t0) = u by cancellation. A^x is open because u + m_E is the open unit ball and |u+m| = 1. Inversion is continuous on E^x because |x^-1 - y^-1| = |x-y|/(|x||y|). All three steps are correctly marked elementary, and proof_deps equals the union of the step uses. Small cases checked: e=0; empty T; one-point T; f=0; E=Q_5, f(t)=5t, t0=1; f(t)=5t^2, t0=0, where q(0)=0 is not a unit, so the exact-valuation hypothesis is needed; changing the uniformizer only scales q by a constant unit. Minor wording I did not change: 'entrywise continuous' is matrix wording carried over from the parent and here just means continuous; 'valuation topology' means the topology of |.|_E, as in the parent.
